Item 1A. Risk Factors

There are numerous factors that affect our business and operating results, many of which are beyond our control. Except as provided below, there are no material changes to the risk factors previously disclosed under the “Risk Factors” section in Oklo’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025.

Growth in artificial intelligence and data-center activity may not result in the demand for our power and heat that we anticipate, and constraints on customer development could adversely affect our business.

Some of our customers and prospective customers operate or otherwise rely on data centers and other similar infrastructure that can support, among other things, the growing demand for technologies that use artificial intelligence. Their business plans, including their construction of or expansion of infrastructure facilities that they intend to power or heat using our offerings, may rely in part on assumptions around AI adoption, computing requirements, energy consumption, and the economic returns on their investments, which may prove to be unwarranted.
Improvements in the efficiency of computing hardware, AI models, software, or cooling systems could reduce the energy required for particular workloads. Changes in computing architectures, including increased use of distributed or on-device processing, could also alter the location, scale, or characteristics of data-center power demand. As a result, even if AI adoption continues to grow, customers’ requirements for additional power or heat may be lower than anticipated or differ from those contemplated by our development plans.

Customers’ and prospective customers’ development plans may also be constrained by reduced availability or increased cost of financing, including concerns about the utilization or economic returns of AI infrastructure. Public opposition or governmental actions concerning electricity costs, grid reliability, water use, land use, or other community impacts could increase development costs or delay, restrict, or prevent data-center projects. These actions could include restrictions on development or interconnection and requirements to fund additional generation or supporting infrastructure.

These developments could cause customers or prospective customers to defer, reduce, relocate, or abandon planned projects, reduce their requirements for our products or services, decline to enter into binding agreements with us, or seek to cancel or renegotiate existing agreements. The resulting reduction or delay in customer commitments could adversely affect our deployment plans and project economics and financing, and could adversely affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

Rapidly evolving energy markets and customer requirements make it difficult to forecast demand for our power and compete effectively.

The markets in which we compete are rapidly evolving. Accordingly, our future financial performance will depend in large part on our ability to adapt to new market demands. The market to supply power for data centers and AI workloads is highly competitive, and growth in spending on these activities does not assure demand for our offerings. Our estimates of the market opportunity, including forecasts of the demand for our power and our ability to capture new spending, are subject to significant uncertainty and are based on assumptions and estimates that may not prove to be accurate. In addition, if customers’ requirements regarding price, location, capacity, delivery timing, or contract duration change, or customers choose other energy solutions, our solutions may not compete as effectively, if at all. Customers may secure alternative power supplies before our powerhouses become available, and their requirements when we are able to deliver power may differ from those reflected in current forecasts. These developments could reduce our ability to obtain long-term customer commitments on terms that support the financing and deployment of our powerhouses. If we are unable to meet the demands of a rapidly evolving market or if our estimates of the market opportunity, including forecasts of the demand for our power, prove to be incorrect, our commercialization may be delayed and our future revenues and cash flows may be lower than anticipated, which could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

42
Table of Contents
The market price of our common stock is, and could remain, highly volatile. Purchasers of our common stock could incur substantial losses.

The trading price of our common stock is, and could remain, volatile and subject to significant fluctuations. The trading price of our common stock depends on many factors, including those described in this “Risk Factors” section, many of which are beyond our control and may not be related to our operating performance. We do not intend to pay cash dividends on our common stock for the foreseeable future.

Furthermore, the stock markets in general have experienced extreme volatility, which has sometimes been unrelated to the operating performance of issuers. The trading price of our common stock may be adversely affected by third parties trying to drive down or drive up the market price. Short sellers and others, some of whom post anonymously on social media, may be positioned to profit if our stock declines or otherwise exhibits volatility, and their activities can negatively affect our stock price and increase the volatility of our stock price. These broad market and industry factors may seriously harm the market price of our common stock, regardless of our operating performance.

Investor expectations regarding the growth of AI and data centers, their associated electricity requirements, and the role of nuclear energy in meeting those requirements may influence the trading price of our common stock. Changes in those expectations, including in response to technological developments, policy changes, or concerns about the financing or economic returns of AI and data-center infrastructure, could adversely affect our stock price even if our business plans, customer relationships, or progress toward commercialization have not changed.

Our ability to deploy our powerhouses and deliver electricity depends in part on obtaining and maintaining interconnection and transmission arrangements, which may be delayed, unavailable or uneconomic.

Certain of our planned powerhouses, including those contemplated for our Ohio campus, will require interconnection to the electric grid and related arrangements with utilities, transmission owners, regional transmission organizations ("RTOs") or independent system operators ("ISOs"). Obtaining these arrangements can involve lengthy studies, technical requirements, financial commitments and regulatory proceedings. Submission or acceptance of an interconnection application, or participation in an interconnection study process, does not assure that a project will obtain interconnection rights, or that the requested capacity or interconnection can be completed on commercially acceptable terms or within our anticipated timelines. Nuclear regulatory authorizations do not themselves provide the grid access or electricity delivery arrangements needed for a project.

Interconnection processes may require us to satisfy technical modeling, site-control, deposit and other requirements within specified deadlines. Deficiencies, changes to a project’s design or capacity, changes in other projects being studied, or changes in applicable requirements may result in additional studies, increased costs, delays or withdrawal of a request from the process. We may also be required to fund or await transmission upgrades, substations or other infrastructure whose cost, availability and completion depend on third parties. Pursuing applications across multiple potential sites does not ensure that any particular project will obtain the interconnection arrangements necessary for deployment.

We have experienced an adverse outcome in this process. FERC denied our complaint challenging PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s ("PJM") withdrawal of an interconnection request for an early-stage potential project in Virginia. That proceeding concerned a request separate from the Ohio campus application. Other pending or future requests may nevertheless encounter similar or different challenges, and we cannot assure favorable outcomes in disputes with utilities, transmission owners, RTOs or ISOs.

The rules and interpretations governing interconnection, transmission service and electricity sales, including the treatment of generation co-located with large electricity users, are subject to change and challenge. Requirements imposed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ("FERC"), state regulators, utilities, RTOs or ISOs could require changes to our proposed configurations or commercial arrangements, impose additional charges or operating restrictions, or limit our ability to serve customers as contemplated. Locating a powerhouse near a customer or behind the customer’s meter does not necessarily eliminate these requirements or the need for supplemental power, backup service or arrangements to export excess electricity. Once interconnected, projects may also be affected by transmission constraints, outages, or curtailment.

These circumstances could delay or prevent deployment, increase development and financing costs, result in unrecoverable expenditures, reduce the capacity we can deliver, or impair our ability to meet customer commitments. They could also
